definition: Dishonest behavior in which someone pretends to think or act one way while secretly doing another.
example: The partner's duplicity surfaced when auditors found a second, hidden set of account books.
nuance: Duplicity means showing one face while hiding another, so it goes beyond telling a single lie, which can be plain dishonesty.
prompt: A teammate promised the captain she would support his new game plan.
options: Her duplicity showed when she cheered the plan in public yet quietly urged others to resist it.
Because of a copier glitch, his duplicity left every player holding two identical playbooks.
In a show of duplicity, she told the captain directly and honestly that she disliked the plan.
Out of duplicity, she stayed late every night drilling the new plays so the plan would work.
reasons: Backing the plan openly while undermining it in secret is exactly this kind of two-faced deceit.
This confuses the word with duplication; a machine making extra copies involves no deceit.
Speaking frankly to someone's face is candor, the reverse of hiding your true position.
Working loyally for the plan shows commitment; nothing here is hidden or false.

practice.prompt: A salesman is bargaining with two rival buyers over the same used car.
options: The salesman made a duplicity of the car's title so each buyer could keep one.
His duplicity impressed both buyers, since he openly shared every offer with each of them.
Out of duplicity, he lowered the price for the buyer who seemed short on money.
His duplicity unraveled when both buyers learned he had promised each of them the lowest price.
reasons: This treats the word as if it meant a copy, mixing it up with duplicate.
Full openness with everyone is honesty, which is the opposite of deceit.
A kind discount involves no pretense, and the word always carries a negative charge.
Making the same secret promise to two rivals is classic double-dealing.
